summary: This article covers the simple science of why a thin metal blade lets skaters glide on ice, how they balance and turn, and how figure skating differs from speed skating.
introduce: Write “Alike” and “Different” at the top of a T-chart on the board and ask students to compare two school subjects in one minute. Explain that “Ice Skating: Gliding on Blades” asks them to make the same kind of comparison.

keyTerms.def: a force that slows down or rubs against something moving across a surface
the top or outside layer of something
a careful, skilled way of doing something

challengeTerms.def: a force pushing on something, often spread over a small area
great accuracy and exactness in doing something
the force that keeps a moving object going

discussion: Do you agree or disagree that ice skating is more about science than most people think? Use evidence from the article to explain.
Explain, in your own words, why a thin ice-skate blade helps a skater glide.
struggling: Pre-teach friction, surface, and technique with pictures or gestures, then let weak readers fill in a T-chart of alike and different with sentence starters.
gifted: Challenge advanced readers to use pressure, precision, and momentum in a short paragraph that compares two ideas from the article and explain which difference matters most.
